variants.name: doobie ConnectionIO program run by a Transactor
variants.idiom_name: ConnectionIO script executed by program.transact(xa) - one transaction per transact
variants.implementation_notes: In the functional Scala stack the script is a description rather than a sequence of side effects: the steps compose in ConnectionIO (or a tagless-final algebra), and xa.transact(program) runs the whole description as a single transaction, with commit or rollback decided by the Transactor's Strategy. The script is a value, so it composes with other programs and can be tested by swapping the interpreter for a rollback-only Transactor; Stream[ConnectionIO, ?] carries the same guarantee for batch scripts. Errors must be raised in the effect (MonadError), not thrown, or the Strategy cannot see them.
pitfalls: Throwing an exception inside ConnectionIO bypasses the Strategy's error handling, so the transaction commits despite the failure.
Replacing the Transactor's Strategy per call (as test fixtures do) changes atomicity silently - the default commits at the end and rolls back on errors.
rawTrans/rawExec skip the transaction wrapper; the all-or-nothing guarantee belongs to transact, not to the program.

variants.name: Play Action with Anorm transaction
variants.implementation_notes: The imperative Play realization: the controller action is the script and Anorm hands it the JDBC connection explicitly - DB.withConnection for read scripts, DB.withTransaction when several statements must commit as one unit (Anorm commits on normal exit and rolls back when an exception escapes the block). Steps are SQL string interpolations with typed parsers, which keeps the script readable and makes it a one-to-one implementation of Fowler's description. Choose it when the team is not on an effect system; the transaction semantics are then the classic JDBC ones plus the pool's.
pitfalls: DB.withConnection may wrap each statement in its own auto-committed transaction, depending on the pool - use withTransaction for multi-statement scripts.
The implicit Connection must not escape the closure: building a Future inside the block that uses it later runs DB work after the transaction ended.
Catching an exception inside the block and returning normally commits partial work.
